note.question: What determines the optimal price and the equilibrium for different levels of information available to customers?
note.overview: The model considers pricing of services with strategic customers who have heterogeneous delay costs motivated by transportation systems. Customers are strategic decision makers who weigh the reward from the transport service against the waiting cost for the vehicle at a transportation station. Customers arrive at the station according to a Poisson process, and the vehicle visits the station according to a renewal process.

source.quote: Methodology/results: We represent the service system as a stochastic clearing process, heterogeneity in delay cost as a random variable, and heterogeneity in rewards as a positive affine transformation of delay cost.
Problem definition: We consider pricing of services with strategic customers who have heterogeneous delay costs motivated by transportation systems.

Guo and Zipkin compared the equilibria for under three levels of information (unobservable, partially observ­ able, and observable) in single-server queues with expo­ nential service times in Guo and Zipkin (2007) and phase-type service times in Guo and Zipkin (2008).

source.section: The Case with Information on the Number of Customers
source.quote: When customers decide, after observing the number of customers already in the system, the expected utility of an arriving customer is affected by the strategies of other customers, so in this model, different from the pre­ vious ones, there are externalities between customers.

In this paper, we take one stylized com­ ponent of the problem that focuses on the trade-off between delays for waiting for the vehicle and the fare versus the benefit from taking the transport, taking into account the fact that potential users in a big city are het­ erogeneous with respect to their sensitivity to delays and possibly with respect to prices.

source.quote: To capture this relation between delay and price sensitivity, we assume that the reward from service is an increasing function of the delay-sensitivity parameter, c.

The nature of customer arrivals (i.e., that they form a Poisson process with rate λ), the distribution F(·) of the intervisit times, the distribution G(·) of the delay-sensitivity parameter C, the parameters r and θ, and the service fee τ are common knowledge to all the customers and the facility administrator, whereas the individual delay-sensitivity parameter c of a cus­ tomer is private information.

We observe that the optimal fee is independent of the arrival rate λ in all cases and increasing in the reward parameter r in all cases except the trivial case, where no customer joins even if the fee is zero.

Unlike the expected total customer utility, the expected administrator revenue may increase, decrease, or remain constant as heterogeneity increases, depending on the expected waiting time and the fee.

To illustrate why this happens, we observe that under the uniform distribution, increasing heterogeneity does not affect the individual expected utilities of the existing types (as there are no externalities) but can increase the total customer utility through the addition of new joining types.

In the system with information on the number of customers, when the fee is fixed and the intervisit time X has a DMRL distribution, a unique equilibrium always exists.
The DMRL condition is implied by the well-known increasing failure rate (IFR) condition and ensures the uniqueness of the equilibrium strategy.
